evidence.text: earth
Phonosemantic compound. 土 represents the meaning and 也 represents the sound.
元气初分，輕清陽爲天，重濁陰爲地。萬物所陳𠛱也。从土也聲。

Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *l'els): semantic 土 (“earth”) + phonetic 也 (OC *laːlʔ). One of the first versions of this character is 𡓬 (> 墬), in which a hill, a pig and a mound of earth are visible; visually, the upper part of the variant is 䧘.
Compare Tibetan གཞི (gzhi, “ground”), Burmese မ္လိယ် (ma.liy) (whence Burmese မြေ (mre, “earth; ground”)) (Hill, 2019). From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *mV-lej.

Possibly the same word as 的, the possessive marker (Wang, 1958), but scholars like Lü (1943) and Yuan et al. (1996) are hesitant about this etymology.
Alternatively, Ōta (2003) proposes that it is a grammaticalization of etymology 1. The construction ADJ + 地 would have semantically developed as follows: "a ADJ place" → "in a ADJ place" → "in a ADJ manner".
元气初分，輕清陽爲天，重濁陰爲地。萬物所陳𠛱也。从土也聲。

evidence.source: Wikimedia Commons transcription of Shuowen Jiezi, 土部
evidence.text: The Eastern Han dictionary entry calls 地 the heavy, turbid yin counterpart to heaven and says it is where the myriad things are arrayed; it analyzes the graph as 从土也聲. This is an early explicit account of 土 as semantic and 也 as phonetic, but is a Han explanation, not direct proof of the graph’s earliest design.
evidence.title: 說文解字/13 - 維基文庫

evidence.field: 地; early graph forms and development
evidence.text: The catalog lists Western Zhou bronze examples (including 縣妀簋 and 㝬簋), Warring States Chu forms, Qin slips, seal forms, and later scripts. Its editorial account reads two Warring States forms as 土 plus 它, and says seal forms regularize the phonetic as 也; it proposes that 它 and 也 were historically close to 土 in sound. This is an explicit competing graphic account, not an independently demonstrated borrowing from a known name for an object depicted by 它. Images are cataloged but were not visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 地字形演变字源_汉字「地」_地的甲骨文_地的金文_金文编_甲骨文编

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 地; form, readings and cited early senses
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 地 as 土 semantic plus 也 phonetic, glosses its basic sense as earth contrasted with heaven, and lists textual examples for ground, cultivated land, territory, place, region, status, distance, and material/texture. It cites 易·繫辭下 for observing the earth, 詩·小雅·斯干 for a girl laid on the ground, and 周禮 for land and territory. Its dated particle example is Song 張先〈八寶裝〉, 厭厭地. These are citations to texts, not independent dates of the underlying composition or surviving manuscript witnesses.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.source: Wiktionary, compiled paleographic and historical phonology tables
evidence.field: 地 and 也; historical pronunciations
evidence.text: The page gives 地 Mandarin dì, Middle Chinese Baxter dijH and Old Chinese Baxter–Sagart *[l]ˤej-s; Zhengzhang Old Chinese *l'els. For 也 it gives Zhengzhang *laːlʔ and lists it in the same phonetic series as 地. Within Zhengzhang’s system and these entries’ scopes, the forms support an approximate sound relationship compatible with a phonetic role; the reconstructions are not direct recordings. The modern readings differ: Standard Mandarin 地 dì versus 也 yě.
evidence.title: 地 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.field: 也; modern pronunciation and origin uncertainty
evidence.text: The entry records Standard Mandarin 也 yě (Pinyin), and its historical-form discussion gives several competing possibilities for the graph’s origin, including a possible snake pictogram, a mouth-related graph, a basin/funnel, and other proposals. The object or original referent of 也 is therefore not established here. That uncertainty does not on its own negate its later independently documented phonetic-series relationship with 地.
evidence.title: 也 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 地; Middle Chinese and Old Chinese pronunciations
evidence.text: The entry records Guangyun fanqie 徒四切 and Middle Chinese 定 initial, 去 tone, 開口三等; Baxter transcription dijH. It lists Old Chinese Baxter–Sagart *[l]ˤej-s and Zhengzhang *l'els, and places 地 under phonetic 也. These comparisons support a historical rather than modern-Mandarin sound relation; the systems and periods must remain distinct.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.source: 漢典 quoting 國語辭典 and classical texts
evidence.field: 地; sense development and attestation examples
evidence.text: The entry separates dì ‘earth/land/place/region/status’ examples from grammatical 地. It cites 易·繫辭下, 詩經·小雅·斯干 (‘乃生女子，載寢之地’), 周禮 and other classical sources for noun senses; it cites Song 張先〈八寶裝〉 for adjective-following 地, and Yuan 西廂記 for the postverbal ‘stand there/remain’ use. This supports attestations of multiple functions but does not establish the precise semantic bridge or first occurrence of each function.
evidence.title: 地 dì、de - 汉典

evidence.source: Wiktionary citing Shi and Li, Language Sciences (2002)
evidence.text: A research-article abstract proposes that grammatical particle de developed from a demonstrative/interrogative pronoun di through analogy with numeral-classifier-noun constructions. It explicitly contrasts this with the common proposal deriving de from 之 by sound change. This is an alternate analysis of the particle’s history, not direct evidence that the locative noun 地 became the manner particle.
evidence.title: The establishment of the classifier system and the grammaticalization of the morphosyntactic particle de in Chinese

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 地 entry citing Wang (1958), Lü (1943), Yuan et al. (1996), Ōta (2003)
evidence.text: The dictionary reports a proposed connection between particle 地 and possessive 的 attributed to Wang, while noting hesitation by Lü and Yuan et al.; it also reports Ōta’s proposed path from ‘an adjective place’ to ‘in an adjective place’ to ‘in an adjective manner.’ This makes the particle etymology disputed. No earliest particle attestation or independently established sequence of those semantic stages was found in inspected material.
evidence.title: 地 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: Digital edition of Shuowen Jiezi with Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.field: 地 and 墬; historical graphic interpretation
evidence.text: The page reproduces Shuowen’s 土+也 account and its 籀文 form 墬, and Duan’s commentary discusses variant textual readings and interprets the graph’s 阜 and 土 elements. This is a historical philological interpretation of the relation between 地 and 墬, not conclusive evidence that 墬 was chronologically the ancestor of 地.
evidence.title: 地 dì、de - 汉典

evidence.source: Kotobank, 普及版 字通 entry
evidence.field: 地; proposed relation to 墬 and graphic replacement
evidence.text: The cited 字通 analysis says 地’s phonetic is 也 and proposes 墬 as an earlier graph for the earth sense, with 地 later made as a phonetic graph after 墬 acquired a falling sense. This is a distinct scholarly proposal; the other inspected references do not establish that chronology as consensus.
evidence.title: 地(チ)とは？ 意味や使い方 - コトバンク

evidence.field: 地; Japanese readings and borrowing claims
evidence.text: The page labels Japanese じ as a Go-on and ち as a Kan-on borrowing from Middle Chinese 地 dijH, while the native kun reading is つち. This separates Sino-Japanese readings from the native Japanese word and does not imply Japanese-origin graph creation.
evidence.title: 地 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫, Chinese University of Hong Kong
evidence.field: 地; form analysis and cited noun/particle uses
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 地 as 土 meaning component plus 也 sound component. It quotes Shuowen’s earth/heaven explanation and cites 易·繫辭下 for earth, 詩·小雅·斯干 for ground, 周禮 for land and territory, 管子 for place, 孟子 for status, Tang 李白 for distance, and Song 張先 for adjective-following 地. These are citations to texts, not independent dates of their compositions or surviving witnesses; they do not establish a complete semantic path.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No visually inspected original inscription images or primary archaeological publication were accessible in this research pass; the form chronology relies on cataloged examples and secondary descriptions.

The claim that early forms use 它 and later forms changed to 也 is reported by a catalog and a secondary discussion. The original referent/name of 它 is not recoverable from inspected evidence, and the sound comparison does not establish an object-name-based whole-graph loan; treat 它’s role as an alleged phonetic form, not as a proven depicted object borrowed for its name.

The first securely inspectable evidence in this pass for 地’s noun sense is traditional Shuowen’s Han-period entry; although bronzes and manuscripts are cataloged, their contexts and readings were not independently examined. No chronology should be inferred from the sequence of modern dictionary glosses.

Sense extensions such as earth → ground/floor → cultivated land/territory → place/region/status/distance/material are supported by cited textual examples, but the exact dates of earliest occurrence and semantic bridges remain unestablished here.

The particle 地 is separately attested in a Song citation and in later sources. Its relation to the noun 地, to 的, or to demonstrative/interrogative forms is disputed; no single derivation or full semantic pathway is demonstrated by the inspected references.

The reconstructions *[l]ˤej-s, *l'els and *laːlʔ are system-specific scholarly reconstructions, not direct attested pronunciations. Their comparison supports but cannot alone prove the original design rationale.

The Han Dian/Shuowen commentary discusses 墬 as 籀文 and textual variants; the Kotobank 字通 interpretation proposes it as an earlier graph for the earth word. Chronological ancestry versus parallel or replaced graph use is not securely resolved.

Several attempted pages were inaccessible (ctext.org returned 403; the CUHK search interface’s image glyphs were not inspectable as pictures). These limits are recorded rather than filled with inferred content.

No primary inscription image or archaeological publication was inspected in this invocation. The Commons candidates are secondary modern redrawings; their source pages identify the underlying records but this pass did not inspect those pixels.

The Xiaoxuetang character query loaded only a generic interface, so no direct database image candidate or specific record page is proposed. Its official CC0 notice was not independently opened in this invocation.
The Shuowen page opened, but extracted text did not reveal the 地 entry during this pass; the dossier already contains a separately documented transcription, which is not fresh verification.

The CUHK examples attest a range of cited noun senses and a Song particle citation, but cited classical works do not by themselves date the surviving wording. The semantic links and earliest attestations remain unresolved.

No new source in this pass independently established the historical sound relation of 地 and 也; use dossier phonology evidence with its system and reconstruction limits. The original referent/name of 也 remains uncertain, without negating its later phonetic role.
The proposed bronze image direct-file URL could not be retrieved by the web tool. The source page nevertheless provided a direct original-file link, but the harness should handle the SVG URL itself.

items.period: Late Western Zhou, associated with 㝬簋
items.caption: A bronze-script form consists of a tall, branching left element beside a more complex right element. The catalog identifies the latter in early forms as 它, while the later Shuowen analysis identifies 也 as the phonetic; this reading of the change is reported, not independently established by the drawing alone.
items.alt: Black drawing of a bronze-script glyph: a tall branching form on the left and a larger, curved, multi-part form on the right.
items.selection_reason: Shows the early form cited in a competing account of the phonetic element, useful for explaining why the received 土-plus-也 analysis does not settle the graph’s earlier components.
items.rights: CC0 1.0, as stated on the Commons page for the representation and its cited Xiaoxuetang source image.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script tradition; dictionary compiled in the Eastern Han (c. 100 CE)
items.caption: The seal-script form has 土 on the left and a rounded, vertically divided element on the right. Shuowen analyzes 地 as 从土也聲, assigning 土 the meaning and 也 the sound; the drawing illustrates that transmitted analysis but does not establish the graph’s earliest design.
items.alt: Black seal-script drawing with a tall left element and a rounded, vertically divided right element.
items.selection_reason: Pairs a visibly different transmitted form with Shuowen’s explicit component analysis, helping explain the established lexicographic account alongside uncertainty about earlier forms.
items.rights: CC0 1.0, as stated on the Commons page; the specific Sinica image is also identified there as CC0.

limitations.text: The bronze form is a modern redraw tied by its catalog description to a late Western Zhou record. Its components and reading have not been independently established from an inspected inscription; the catalog’s 它-to-也 account remains a reported interpretation.

Shuowen’s 土-plus-也 analysis is an Eastern Han lexicographic account, not direct proof of the graph’s earliest design. The relation between 地 and the related form 墬 is also not securely established as chronological ancestry.
